newsitem.title: USA: Smoking caused one in five Florida deaths - study.
newsitem.headline: Smoking caused one in five Florida deaths - study.

text.p: One out of five deaths in Florida in 1995 was linked to tobacco, making smoking the single most common cause of death in the state, Florida health officials said on Thursday.

Of 151,619 deaths recorded in 1995, 31,024 were linked to tobacco-related diseases such as lung cancer, heart disease, stroke and other illnesses, according to a report released by the Florida Department of Health.

The average years of life estimated to have been lost by those who died was more than 12 years. State health officials, who, under Gov. Lawton Chiles have been on an anti-smoking crusade, said smoking related mortality eclipsed all other causes of death in the department's survey, which used computer models developed by the Centres for Disease Control and Prevention to analyse the data.

Health officials said the findings mirrored earlier studies across the United States that pointed to cigarette smoking as the nation's No. 1 health risk, responsible for the deaths of hundreds of thousands of Americans every year.

"But that's not the whole story, because people may be suffering from emphysema, chronic bronchitis and other ... illnesses attributed to tobacco before they actually die," said Dr. James Howell, Florida's secretary of health. "This is a tremendous public health problem."

Anti-smoking advocates used Thursday's release to kick off a year-long anti-smoking crusade they said would enlist the volunteer help of 500,000 Floridians across the state. The campaign came as Chiles tried to drum up support for a 10-cent per pack tax on cigarettes, the proceeds of which would be used to fund education and prevention programmes for young people.
